title: The Seychelles Saga
subtitle: 8 days, four idiots, one rental car and a tortoise named Obama

content:
“Mattu, let’s go somewhere—I’m going to be bored,” my wife declared one night, right after

deciding to take a two-month career break.

I nodded like a man with a plan (who just Googled ‘countries with no visa for Indians’ five minutes ago)

“Hmmm… sure. Let’s go. Seychelles doesn’t need a visa anyway.”

15/06/2025

The Forever Journey

We boarded our late-night flight from Bengaluru, sleepy but excited, with a generous 10-hour layover in Mumbai. From Mumbai, it was a direct Indigo flight to Mahé. We landed around lunchtime

Rinku, the planner, had tweaked our itinerary to head straight to Praslin instead of staying in Mahe. So we grabbed a quick lunch at the Mahé airport—which had barely any options—and headed to the port via taxi.

That’s where I got my first taste of vacation math: 40 Euros for the taxi.
Instant conversion mode: EUR to INR... ouch. Anxiety spiked.

“Relax, bud,” I whispered to my inner-me and paid cash

Then came the ferry—an hour-long ride to Praslin.
And let me tell you, they run that port like it’s an airport.
Checked-in luggage? ✅
Boarding pass? ✅


Once we docked at Praslin, it was a breeze. We rented a self-driving car right from the port parking lot for about 35 EUR per day. Total win.
The freedom of wheels in a new place? Unbeatable.


Grabbed a few groceries for the rest of our stay and drove straight to our stay—Stone Self Catering, a cozy B&B at Praslin Centre.

16/06/2025

Exploring Praslin (aka "Praaaleee")

Btw, Praslin is pronounced Praaaleeee.
(Just putting it out there before someone like Fariniii corrects you on the beach)


I woke up around 8 AM, if I remember vaguely. Harini and Rinku were already up and moving. Right opposite our BnB, Stone Self Catering, was Grand Anse Beach. I took a quick stroll and jogged along the shore for a few hundred meters. Definitely a good start—the inner me gave a rare nod of approval.


After grabbing a sumptuous breakfast of fresh, juicy fruits, boiled eggs, and a bit of Semiya, we set off to explore Anse Georgette.

The Unexpected Hike

“Do we really have to walk a mile?” I asked as soon as someone told us to park our car near the Lemuria Golf Gate, where Google Maps showed 1.8 km to the destination.

Apparently, entry into the golf course is only allowed for guests staying there. The rest of us? We had to walk along the course to reach the beach.

It was quite tiring, with a good amount of uphill climb. We took around 30 minutes to finally reach Anse Georgette.

“Woah… stunning,” we all exclaimed as the view unfolded—turquoise blue waters, crystal-clear waves, and powdery white sand. Postcard material.

Anse means bay in Seychellois Creole. All the beaches have Anse either in prefix or suffix.

Anse Georgette had barely any people, which made it feel even more special. Rinku and I jumped into the water and played for more than an hour, while the wives stayed near the shore—thanks to the slightly rough waves.

After some good playtime and chilling on the sand, we started back toward Praslin City.

Things in Seychelles wind down pretty early—most shops and restaurants close by 6 PM, so we had a few things to rush through:

  • Currency exchange

  • Lunch

  • Check out travel agencies for the next day’s island trip

But by the time we returned, it was a little too late for lunch. We grabbed some fish curry and rice from a nearby takeaway. Of course, we had a couple of vegetarians on board, so we threw in some pizza to balance the meal.

Unfortunately, most travel agencies had already shut for the day.

Sunset at Anse Lazio

Post lunch, we freshened up and drove towards the eastern side of the island to catch the sunset at Anse Lazio—a spot many people had recommended.

We reached around 5:50 PM and rushed to the beach. And wow—what a sight.

The sky was painted in deep orange hues, boats were swaying gently with the waves, and the sun was setting in a way that was almost surreal. It was one of those “this-is-why-we-travel” moments.

“Macha, we have to come back here and play,” Rinku said, clearly not satisfied with just watching

the sunset. Fair enough.

So we decided to come back a day later after our island tour, pack lunch, and do a beach picnic.

We clicked a few silhouette shots and took a slow, scenic drive back around the island.

There were a few takeaways here and there, but otherwise, everything was shut. Honestly, the kind of work-life balance they have here is admirable.

Jack Takeaway & Café: Late-Night Saviour

We ended the night at Jack Takeaway & Café—probably the biggest takeaway joint on the island. It had a good variety of options at “relatively affordable” prices. Well, as affordable as it gets in Seychelles.

A burger cost 100 SCR (about ₹600). That’s the cheapest item.

While waiting for our order, we met a couple on their honeymoon—Vignesh and Nevetha—from Chennai, currently living in Mumbai. We exchanged a few formal greetings and got chatting. Turned out they had booked an island tour for the next day.

On the fly, I opened GetYourGuide, found the same operator, and booked our slot.

We exchanged numbers, agreed to meet the next day, and wrapped up the evening.

17/06/2025 - Giant Tortoises, Snorkeling & Obama the Explorer

So this was Day 3—the much-awaited Island Tour Day, where we were set to explore Curieuse Island, the natural habitat of the giant Aldabra tortoises, and St. Pierre Island, famous for its snorkelling spots.

We were ready by 7:30 AM, waiting for Island Tours to pick us up. We coordinated with Vignesh and Nevetha—they were also on the way, and we met them at the port.

We all boarded the same boat, and it took around an hour to reach Curieuse Island.

Curieuse Island & the Tale of Obama the Tortoise

Once we arrived at Curieuse Island, we were welcomed by our guide, Alex, a warm, knowledgeable guy who seemed to know every leaf and tortoise on the island by name.

He started by giving us a short but fascinating briefing about the giant Aldabra tortoises, the conservation research happening there, and how we should respectfully interact with these majestic creatures.

To avoid the crowd at the tortoise zone, Alex gave us about 20–30 minutes to enjoy the beach and surroundings before we began a guided hike to the other side of the island—where most of the tortoises freely roam in their natural habitat.

As we started hiking, Alex casually began unraveling the island’s layered history. He shared stories about how Curieuse was once hit by a plague/some disease—something we had no idea about. It added a completely different lens to the place, beyond just the palm trees and beaches

Along the way, we spotted a variety of colourful crabs crawling around, blending in with the sand and mangrove roots. At one point, Alex even caught one, held it up like a wildlife presenter. Simple moments like that made the walk way more fun and memorable.

Curieuse is unique in that it’s a true sanctuary for these tortoises—you can see them moving about freely, with no barriers or fences.

And then came the star of the island: a tortoise named Obama.

What’s unique about him? Well, unlike the rest of the herd, Obama prefers solitude. He had once wandered from one side of the island to the other—a six-month journey—alone. The conservationists took him back, but to their surprise, he returned again within three weeks, this time bringing a friend. Clearly, Obama had a taste for solo adventures and preferred his own corner of the island. So, they let him be—and there he was, slowly walking in to greet us. A true island legend.

After some time at the beach, we began a short hike to the other side of the island, where we were greeted by 50-60 giant tortoises just casually existing in the wild. It was surreal.

We even saw tiny baby tortoises—some just a day old—being cared for in a separate enclosure. We clicked tons of pictures, fed some leaves to the tortoises, and soaked in the rare experience.

BBQ + Snorkel = Island Life

Soon after, a barbecue lunch was arranged—it was delicious and much needed after all that walking.

Next up: snorkelling. We changed, hopped back on the boat, and headed toward the snorkelling point, about 15–20 minutes away.

With life jackets on and snorkel masks in place, we splashed into the water. We saw plenty of zebra fish, vibrant corals, and even a giant sea urchin. And then came the moment of the day

Rinku popped up, eyes wide: “Macha, I saw a stingray!”

Technically, the plan was to snorkel at St. Pierre Island, too. But the guide, after assessing our swimming confidence, advised against it—the tides were rough, and snorkeling without life jackets there was risky.

Still, he took us there to enjoy the view. And what a view it was. The rocky formations in the middle of the ocean were spectacular.

↗ View this post on Instagram

We clicked some more pictures and then made our way back to Praslin. By the time we got back to our Airbnb, it was around 5 PM.

We had initially planned to go back to Anse Lazio to catch the sunset again, but it didn’t make sense anymore. It’s a 45-minute drive, and the sunset would’ve been long gone by the time we got there. So we decided to skip the chase and just chill.

We relaxed for a while, had some great conversations, and then headed to Jack Takeaway. Thankfully, it wasn’t as crowded as the previous day, and we found plenty of seating.

We enjoyed a good meal, reflected on the day, and finally wrapped things up.

18/06/2025 - Coco de Mer, Beach Picnics & The Good Kind of Nothing

Yet another slow, relaxing day in paradise. The plan was to visit Vallée de Mai, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and natural reserve that’s home to Seychelles’ iconic Coco de Mer—the world’s largest nut, which resembles human genitals. No one says it out loud, but everyone’s thinking it.

“Macha, it’s so expensive,” I said, looking at the ticket price to Vallee de Mai.

“What are the other options?” Cutti asked

Vignesh had mentioned they visited Fond Ferdinand, a similar reserve, smaller but much cheaper.

Eventually, we decided to skip both. Spending thousands to see a single nut felt a bit… nutty. So we chose the budget traveller route—drive around the area, especially near Vallée de Mai, and look out for Coco de Mers in their natural habitat.

Guess what? We found a couple of them just like that. Victory!

Picnic at Anse Lazio

We grabbed pizza and some seafood for lunch and drove toward Anse Lazio. Spread out our sheets, laid down our pizza and fried fish with some rice under a shady coconut tree. Honestly, it felt like something out of a luxury travel ad - White sand. Blue water. Lunch with a view.

Rinku and I headed into the water for over an hour, floating, chatting, and randomly getting philosophical about life—total mood.

As the sun began to set, we performed the travel ritual, posing and clicking a few dozen pictures. Such a slow life, and every bit deserved.

Evening Farewell at Jack’s

On our way back, we made one last stop at our beloved Jack Takeaway. Tried a local drink made from passion fruit and orange, alongside some fried rice and noodles. Jack’s food really is something you shouldn’t miss. And if you're into pizza, don’t forget the pizzeria next to it.

19/06/2025 - La Digue – The Island That Catfished Our Expectations

Today was nothing like the previous slow day—we had to rush to catch our ferry to La Digue. We took the first ferry in the morning and reached around 9 AM.

As we arrived, I looked around and thought: “Wait, no motorcycles on the island?”

That’s what all the travel blogs had promised. But reality? We saw trucks, pickup vehicles, and—yep—construction sites everywhere. The tourism boom had changed things.

We checked into Villa Antique—and let me mention the name boldly so that YOU NEVER BOOK IT.

The host was super sweet… until we paid. After that? Radio silence.

Our room had tiny creepy worms, and when we complained, she flat-out refused to change the sheets or the room, saying we had “already checked in.”

“WTF?!”

We had no other option, so we cleaned up ourselves. And to top it off, the rooms didn’t have proper latches. Not even the bathrooms.

Thank God it was just me and my wife in there. 😅

Anyway, we decided to make the most of it. We hired gear cycles, which immediately unlocked some childhood nostalgia.

“Macha, first time I’m riding a gear cycle. It was my dream as a kid.”

“Same macha, I didn’t have one either.”

“Yeah, me too,” chimed in the wives.

It was wholesome. Like we were all cycling through forgotten corners of our childhoods.

Anse Source d’Argent & The Transparent Kayak Scam

We pedaled to our first beach—Anse Source d’Argent. Took us about 20 minutes.

After parking the bikes, we bought tickets for a transparent kayak experience scheduled for later in the day, and went straight to the beach.

You’ve got to walk across the shore to find the good spots. And wow—the giant granite boulders, naturally sculpted and colored, gave the beach a mystical, otherworldly vibe. Easily the reason why it’s called one of the best beaches in the world.

While Rinku splashed around, Farini worked on her perfect poses, and my “kid” (aka my wife) began collecting seashells and shiny rocks like a beach goblin. I just laid back and napped on the sand for a bit. By noon, we were ready for our kayak ride. It was hot and overhyped.

They took us a short distance from shore, dropped us off with the transparent kayak, and said, “Go explore.”

No real coral views, no marine life like they promised. Just hot sun and a mildly cool boat.

Our guide? Grumpy. He took the worst “complimentary pictures” ever—blurry, poorly framed, and full of attitude.

Tip: If you want to do kayaking here, book a proper package that includes snorkel + island exploration. Not this rushed ride.

We ran into Vignesh and Nevetha again, and they said their package experience was amazing. So yeah, lesson learned.

We cycled back and grabbed dinner at Le Repaire —delicious, fresh, and satisfying. A much-needed mood lifter.

Honestly? La Digue didn’t live up to the hype.

As an island, it’s beautiful—no doubt. But the hospitality, experience, and overall vibe were a letdown. At least for us.

Would we recommend it? Maybe. But with a strong disclaimer: choose your stay wisely, and book proper experiences in advance.

20/06/2025 - North Island, Stone Beaches & One Grand Finale

Zzzzzz, zzzzz, my phone buzzed relentlessly.
“Macha, let’s go?” Rinku’s voice on the other end

I had totally forgotten that we planned to explore the northern side of the island before the sun peeked over the horizon.

Half asleep, we slipped into our beachwear, hopped on our bicycles, and started pedalling towards the northern beaches. Our first stop was the famous Anse Severe, known for its beachside shacks. But since it was only 8 in the morning, everything was shut tight. Of course.

We parked our cycles and thought we’d try playing around a bit, but the beach had too many stones—not exactly play-friendly. So, we strolled along the shore, soaking in the early morning calm, before heading further up to Anse Patates.

Now that one was beautiful.

It was a small, curved shoreline—almost like a private little crescent carved into the island. We played in the water for a bit, snapped some pictures, and headed back just in time to catch our free breakfast. If nothing else, at least we were gonna get our money’s worth out of that shady hotel.

Me and Cutti showed up twinning in our outfits while Rinku and Farini followed in later. The path to Grand Anse was something else—once you leave the main town behind, you pass through a semi-dense forest trail. Some parts are even fenced off because of the deep slopes, but the entire walk builds anticipation.

And then—boom—the trail opens up to one of the most breathtaking beaches we’d seen.

Grand Anse truly lived up to its name.

At one end, giant brown boulders framed the blue ocean in perfect contrast. We laid down our beach mats, relaxed under the setting sun, and even did some sand art—because why not?

As dusk settled, we grabbed some delicious takeaway from a nearby shack and made our way back. With early morning ferries calling us back to Mahe the next day, we packed up our bags and said our goodnights.

21/06/2025 - Morne Blanc Hike & Sunset at Beau Vallon

On our second last day, we arrived back in Mahé and picked up a rental car directly from the port. After navigating the island roads, we reached our BnB—only to realise it was located in the southern part of the island, quite far from most of the places we had planned to visit. Almost everything we wanted to see was up north, which meant longer travel times than we had expected. Not ideal, but we adjusted.

We rested for a bit and then around noon decided to try the Morne Blanc trail. Cutti and Farini weren’t too keen on it—especially after reading reviews that mentioned how steep and difficult the trail was—so we dropped them off at Beau Vallon Beach and drove to the starting point of the hike.

When we reached, we weren’t even sure we were in the right place. There was just a board by the side of the road marking the trailhead unlike a proper parking spot or entrance vibes. We parked our car at the edge and started the hike.

The trail was steep—about 600 meters of elevation in under 800 meters of distance. It was intense. Halfway through, the weather took a turn and it started raining. We were already halfway up, so we continued despite the slippery path.

We finally reached the top, expecting to be rewarded with the famous view. But unfortunately, all we could see was fog—thick and dense. The view was completely covered. Still, the experience of the hike, the rain, and the unexpected weather made it memorable in its own way.

After a short rest at the top, we began the descent. It was slippery and quite tricky, but we made it down safely. By then, it was past 5 PM. We picked up Cutti and Farini and went back to Beau Vallon to catch the sunset.

The sunset didn’t disappoint. Clear skies, vibrant colours, and a peaceful beach atmosphere made it one of the best we’d seen. We also met up with Vignesh and his wife again (this time it was actually planned), and ended the day with some good conversations and an delicious meal at Lobster Bay.

A tiring day, but definitely one of the highlights of the trip.

22/06/2025 - Wrapping Up

On our final day, we had planned to visit the Takamaka Rum Distillery, which was quite close to our stay. Seemed like a fitting way to end the trip. But turns out—it was Sunday, and the distillery was closed.

So, change of plans. We took it slow, woke up late, cooked a nice meal at our BnB, packed up, and stepped out to buy some souvenirs. After that, we made our way to the airport.

As our flight took off from Mahé, the view of the turquoise waters below made it all sink in. The trip had come to an end—but it had been an unforgettable one.

From postcard-perfect beaches and island hikes to spontaneous meetups and some seriously good food, Seychelles gave us a lot to hold on to.

Back to Bengaluru, back to routine—but a part of us definitely stayed back on those blue shores.

Travellers - The Forever Four

places.name: Anse Georgette
places.why: Hidden beach — worth the 30-minute uphill walk past the golf course.

places.name: Anse Lazio
places.why: Best spot for sunset and a beach picnic.

places.name: Curieuse Island
places.why: Giant Aldabra tortoises roaming free — including Obama, the solo explorer.

places.name: Anse Source d'Argent
places.why: Those giant sculpted granite boulders make it otherworldly.

places.name: Grand Anse, La Digue
places.why: Forest trail opens to the most breathtaking beach we saw — perfect for sand art.

places.name: Morne Blanc
places.why: Steep but memorable — we got fog instead of the famous view.

items: Rent a car in Praslin & Mahé (~€35/day) — freedom is unbeatable.
Ferries run like airports: boarding passes and luggage check-in. Book in advance.
Keep EUR cash handy — taxi from Mahé airport to port is €40.
Shops and restaurants shut by 6 PM; Jack Takeaway & Café is the late-night saviour.
Budget ₹600 for a burger, ₹1000–1500 for a meal.
On La Digue, choose your stay wisely and avoid Villa Antique.
Transparent kayak is overrated unless booked with a proper snorkel package.
Start the Morne Blanc hike early to beat the rain and clouds.
Skip pricey Vallée de Mai (€25); Fond Ferdinand is cheaper, or just spot Coco de Mer from roadside trees.
Sunday = everything closed, including the Takamaka Rum Distillery — plan souvenirs ahead.
Stock groceries and snacks beforehand; after 6 PM the islanders simply vanish.
